notes: SECOND PASS redraft, built from scratch per the adversarial-fact-check corrections supplied. All flagged issues addressed: (1) Jehoash/Joash of Israel is now role:manager with NO parentManagerId (arrow ritual 13:14-19, recovers three cities 13:25, defeats Amaziah 14:8-14 — genuinely tier-worthy on his own). (2) Shalmaneser V added as a full manager tier — he personally besieges and captures Samaria (17:3-6), the event that ends the northern kingdom; given comparable weight to Sennacherib/Nebuchadnezzar. (3) 2 Kings 20:12 uses KJV's own spelling "Berodachbaladan" (NOT the Isaiah 39:1 parallel-account spelling). (4) Zedekiah's final siege corrected to ~18 months (9th year/10th month to 11th year/4th month per 25:1-3), not "over two years". (5) Jehoram of Judah's genealogy entry now states directly that Jehoram of Israel is Athaliah's own brother (both children of Ahab), making him Jehoram of Judah's direct brother-in-law — no longer routed through Ahaziah of Israel. (6) Pul (15:19) and Tiglathpileser (15:29, 16:7) are kept as two separate character entries; the identification is explicitly flagged as coming from 1 Chronicles 5:26, a different book, not stated as same-book fact. (7) Naming collision flagged: Jehu the king (chs 9-10) vs. the earlier prophet Jehu son of Hanani (1 Kings 16:1,7) — different people, different books, same name. (8) Evilmerodach's parentage: 2 Kings 25:27 never states Nebuchadnezzar is his father — set to null/hedged with an explicit caveat, consistent with how this project handles other unstated-in-this-book parentage. ADDITIONAL COLLISIONS CAUGHT ON RE-SCAN (not in the original flagged list, added per the standing instruction to re-scan every name): Jehoahaz of Israel (13:1-9, son of Jehu) vs. Jehoahaz of Judah (23:31, son of Josiah) — completely different men, ~80 years apart, same name. Shallum son of Jabesh (king of Israel, 15:10-15) vs. Shallum husband of Huldah the prophetess (22:14) — both within this same book. "Zachariah"/"Zechariah": 2 Kings itself spells BOTH its own occurrences "Zachariah" (15:8, son of Jeroboam II; 18:2, Hezekiah's maternal grandfather) — kept as two distinct "Zachariah" entries, both flagged as a different spelling/person from "Zechariah" the writing prophet or other Zechariahs elsewhere in scripture. "Jeremiah of Libnah" (23:31, 24:18, father of queens Hamutal) is explicitly NOT the prophet Jeremiah — flagged. "Elah" (father of Hoshea, 15:30/17:1) flagged against King Elah of Israel in 1 Kings 16 (different book, different person). KJV spellings preserved throughout: "Pharaohnechoh" (one word, 23:29ff.), "Evilmerodach" (one word, 25:27), "Tiglathpileser" (one word), "Benhadad" (one word — scripture never numbers him "II", that's a scholarly convention, not asserted here as book fact). No role:"law" tier was used for this book — 2 Kings is regnal-narrative genre throughout; its closest law-adjacent material (17:7-23's theological indictment explaining Israel's fall, and 22-23's rediscovered book of the law) is folded into the relevant kings' own manager entries as narrative content they personally enact, not treated as a standalone law/theme tier, since forcing one would misrepresent the book's actual genre balance.

characters.name: Elijah

genealogy.note: Elijah's own lineage is not given in 2 Kings (introduced without patronymic already in 1 Kings 17:1 as 'Elijah the Tishbite'); this book only covers the close of his ministry.

verses.note: calls down fire from heaven on two captains of fifty sent by Ahaziah of Israel
parts the Jordan by smiting it with his rolled-up mantle
taken up by a whirlwind into heaven in a chariot and horses of fire, witnessed by Elisha

funFacts: His mantle, dropped as he ascends, becomes the sign of Elisha's succession (2:13-14).
2 Kings 1 is entirely about his confrontation with Ahaziah of Israel over consulting Baalzebub, god of Ekron, instead of the LORD.

characters.name: Ahaziah (king of Israel)
characters.perkNote: His refusal to consult the LORD is the entire occasion for Elijah's final recorded confrontation.

genealogy.father: Ahab (per 1 Kings 22:40, 51; not restated by name in 2 Kings 1 itself)
genealogy.note: Son of Ahab and, by extension, Jezebel; brother of Jehoram/Joram of Israel and of Athaliah.

verses.note: falls through a lattice in his upper chamber in Samaria and is injured
dies according to Elijah's word for consulting Baalzebub the god of Ekron; succeeded by his brother Jehoram (Joram), 'because he had no son'

funFacts: NAMING COLLISION FLAG: a second, unrelated 'Ahaziah' — king of Judah — appears later in this same book (2 Kings 8-9). They are different men from different kingdoms; do not conflate.

characters.name: Elisha

genealogy.note: Called from plowing behind twelve yoke of oxen; his call itself is narrated in 1 Kings 19:19-21, not this book.

verses.note: asks for and receives a double portion of Elijah's spirit; parts the Jordan with Elijah's fallen mantle
multiplies a widow's oil to pay her debts
raises the Shunammite woman's son
instructs Naaman to wash seven times in Jordan
prays open the eyes of his servant to see horses and chariots of fire surrounding them
a dead man is revived when his corpse touches Elisha's bones, after Elisha's own death

funFacts: His ministry spans the reigns of at least five kings of Israel (Jehoram through Jehoash) plus interactions with Judah and Syria — the longest single narrative thread in 2 Kings.
2 Kings 2:23-24 (youths mocking his baldness, mauled by two she-bears) is genuinely in the text; it is not omitted here, just noted rather than dwelt on.

characters.name: Gehazi
characters.perkNote: His greed after Naaman's healing is a cautionary counter-example within Elisha's tier.

genealogy.note: Identified only as Elisha's servant.

verses.note: secretly pursues Naaman for silver and garments, lies to Elisha about it, and is struck with Naaman's leprosy
recounts Elisha's great deeds to 'the king' (contextually most likely Jehoram of Israel, though the text names him only as 'the king')

characters.name: The Shunammite woman
characters.perkNote: Hosts and provisions Elisha, prompting the promise of a son.

genealogy.note: Never named in the text, only 'a great woman' of Shunem; her husband is likewise unnamed.
children: an unnamed son, born and later raised from death (2 Kings 4:17, 4:34-35)

verses.note: builds Elisha a chamber on the wall so he can lodge when passing through
her son dies suddenly and is raised by Elisha
her land is restored by the king (Jehoram of Israel, contextually) after a seven-year famine, on Gehazi's testimony

characters.name: The widow of a son of the prophets
characters.perkNote: Her cry for help occasions the oil miracle.

genealogy.note: Unnamed; wife of a deceased 'son of the prophets' who owed a creditor.
children: two unnamed sons, about to be taken as bondsmen for debt (2 Kings 4:1)

verses.note: Elisha multiplies her small pot of oil to fill many borrowed vessels, enabling her to pay her debt

characters.name: Benhadad (king of Syria)
characters.perkNote: Recurring antagonist across several Elisha episodes; his campaigns are repeatedly frustrated by Elisha's word.

genealogy.note: 2 Kings gives no patronymic for this Benhadad. Scholars sometimes number him 'Benhadad II' to distinguish him from an earlier Syrian king of the same name in 1 Kings 15/20, but scripture itself never applies a numeral — not asserted here as book fact.

verses.note: besieges Samaria, causing a severe famine
falls sick in Damascus and sends Hazael to inquire of Elisha
smothered to death by Hazael with a wet cloth; Hazael reigns in his stead

funFacts: KJV spells his name as one word, 'Benhadad', throughout.

characters.name: The four leprous men at the gate

genealogy.note: Unnamed as individuals; an undifferentiated group of four, kept together per this project's rule against inventing distinctions the text doesn't support.

verses.note: during the Syrian siege of Samaria, discover the enemy camp abandoned and report the news, ending the famine

funFacts: Load-bearing to the resolution of the siege narrative even though none of the four is individually named.

characters.name: Naaman

genealogy.note: Captain of the host of the king of Syria; no patronymic given. Wife is mentioned but unnamed; his household included a captive Israelite servant girl who first told him of Elisha.

verses.note: introduced as 'a great man... honourable... but he was a leper'
dips in Jordan seven times per Elisha's instruction and his flesh is restored
confesses the LORD, asks forgiveness in advance for bowing in the house of Rimmon with his master, and departs with Elisha's blessing 'Go in peace'

funFacts: His entire chapter is self-contained: healing, conversion, and Gehazi's punishment all resolve within ch. 5.

characters.name: Jehoram (Joram), king of Israel

genealogy.note: Son of Ahab; reigned after his brother Ahaziah died childless (1:17). Sister: Athaliah, also a child of Ahab, who married Jehoram of Judah — making Jehoram of Israel Jehoram of Judah's own brother-in-law directly, not through any intermediate relation.

verses.note: begins to reign; put away the pillar of Baal his father had made, but did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam
joins Jehoshaphat of Judah and the king of Edom against rebelling Moab; Elisha provides water in trenches
killed by Jehu, who shoots him through the heart with an arrow in the field of Naboth the Jezreelite

funFacts: NAMING COLLISION FLAG: 'Jehoram'/'Joram' is used interchangeably in the text for this king AND for Jehoram of Judah, his brother-in-law, reigning at the same time in the neighboring kingdom — two different men.

characters.name: Jehoram, king of Judah

genealogy.note: King of Judah; married Athaliah, daughter of Ahab (8:18) — making him brother-in-law to Jehoram of Israel directly, since Jehoram of Israel is Athaliah's own brother (both children of Ahab). Father of Ahaziah of Judah.

verses.note: begins to reign; 'walked in the way of the kings of Israel... for the daughter of Ahab was his wife'
Edom and Libnah revolt from Judah in his days
dies and is succeeded by his son Ahaziah

funFacts: Distinct from Jehoram/Joram, king of Israel, his own brother-in-law and contemporary — same name, different kingdom.

characters.name: Mesha, king of Moab
characters.perkNote: His rebellion is the occasion for the joint Israel-Judah-Edom campaign.

genealogy.note: No genealogy given beyond 'king of Moab... a sheepmaster'.
children: his eldest son, offered as a burnt offering upon the wall (2 Kings 3:27)

verses.note: rendered tribute of lambs and wool to Israel, then rebelled after Ahab's death
when the battle goes against him, offers his eldest son as a burnt offering on the city wall

characters.name: Jehoshaphat, king of Judah
characters.perkNote: Allies with Jehoram of Israel for the Moab campaign, as he had with Ahab in 1 Kings.

genealogy.father: Asa (established in 1 Kings 22:41-42, not restated here)
genealogy.note: His own full reign is recorded in 1 Kings 22; 2 Kings only shows his cameo joining the Moab campaign.

verses.note: agrees to join Jehoram of Israel against Moab: 'I am as thou art, my people as thy people'
asks for a prophet of the LORD, leading to Elisha's involvement

funFacts: NAMING COLLISION FLAG: Jehu the king's own father is separately named 'Jehoshaphat, the son of Nimshi' (9:2, 9:14) — an entirely unrelated man who happens to share this king's name.

characters.name: Jehu, king of Israel

genealogy.note: His father Jehoshaphat son of Nimshi is NOT King Jehoshaphat of Judah — a same-name, different-person collision within this book's own genealogical notices.

verses.note: anointed king over Israel by a young prophet sent from Elisha, commissioned to strike down the house of Ahab
identified from a distance by his driving: 'the driving is like the driving of Jehu... he driveth furiously'
destroys Baal worship out of Israel
yet did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam

funFacts: NAMING COLLISION FLAG: an earlier, unrelated prophet also named Jehu — Jehu the son of Hanani — appears in 1 Kings 16:1,7, delivering oracles against Baasha. Different man, different book, same name.

characters.name: Jezebel
characters.perkNote: Her death under Jehu's order closes out the judgment on Ahab's house.

genealogy.note: Widow of Ahab; her fuller history is in 1 Kings. Mother of Ahaziah, Jehoram (Joram) of Israel, and Athaliah.
spouses: Ahab (established in 1 Kings, not restated here)

verses.note: paints her face and tires her head, is thrown down from a window by her own servants at Jehu's word, and trodden underfoot
only her skull, feet, and palms of her hands are found, per Elijah's earlier prophecy (1 Kings 21:23)

characters.name: Jehonadab (Jonadab), son of Rechab
characters.perkNote: Rides publicly with Jehu, lending visible support to the purge.

genealogy.note: Ancestor of the Rechabite family/clan; his own fuller story is not given here.

verses.note: meets Jehu, gives him his hand, and rides with him in his chariot 'to see my zeal for the LORD'
present with Jehu inside the house of Baal during the purge of Baal worshippers

characters.name: Ahaziah, king of Judah

genealogy.note: Grandson of Ahab and Jezebel through his mother; nephew of Jehoram/Joram, king of Israel.

verses.note: begins to reign at age twenty-two, in Jerusalem
visits his uncle-by-marriage Jehoram of Israel at Jezreel while Jehoram recovers from wounds
flees Jehu's purge, is wounded near Ibleam, and dies at Megiddo

funFacts: NAMING COLLISION FLAG: a wholly different 'Ahaziah' — king of Israel — appears earlier in this same book (2 Kings 1). Different kingdom, different man, same name.

characters.name: Athaliah

genealogy.father: Ahab (2 Kings 8:18; called 'daughter of Omri', Ahab's father, in 8:26 — a common dynastic usage, not a separate paternity claim)
genealogy.note: Sister of Ahaziah and of Jehoram (Joram), kings of Israel — both sons of Ahab. Wife of Jehoram of Judah, mother of Ahaziah of Judah.

verses.note: upon her son Ahaziah's death, destroys all the royal seed of the house of Judah to seize the throne
reigns over the land for six years while the infant Joash is hidden
cries 'Treason, Treason' upon discovering the coup, and is put to death

funFacts: The only woman to reign in her own right over either kingdom in the books of Kings.

genealogy.note: High priest; no patronymic given in 2 Kings.
spouses: Jehosheba, per the parallel account in 2 Chronicles 22:11 — not stated as marriage within 2 Kings itself, noted here only as a cross-book detail, not asserted as this book's own fact

verses.note: makes a covenant with the captains of hundreds to protect and crown the hidden child Joash
arms the guard with David's shields and spears kept in the temple, and crowns Joash
makes a covenant between the LORD, the king, and the people
Joash 'did that which was right... all his days, wherein Jehoiada the priest instructed him'

characters.name: Jehosheba
characters.perkNote: Physically hides the infant Joash, making Jehoiada's later coup possible at all.

genealogy.note: Daughter of King Jehoram of Judah, sister of Ahaziah of Judah; 2 Kings does not itself state she was Jehoiada's wife (that detail is only in 2 Chronicles 22:11, a different book).

verses.note: takes the infant Joash and hides him from Athaliah's purge for six years

characters.name: Joash (Jehoash), king of Judah

verses.note: began to reign at age seven
has a chest bored with a hole set beside the altar to collect money for temple repairs
strips the temple and his own treasures to pay off Hazael of Syria and avert an attack on Jerusalem
slain by his own servants in a conspiracy at the house of Millo

funFacts: NAMING COLLISION FLAG: 'Joash'/'Jehoash' is also the name of a later, unrelated king of Israel (2 Kings 13-14) — different kingdom, different man, same alternating name-form.

characters.name: Jozachar, son of Shimeath
characters.perkNote: One of two servants who assassinate Joash of Judah.

verses.note: named as one of the two servants who killed Joash of Judah

characters.name: Jehozabad, son of Shomer
characters.perkNote: The second of two servants who assassinate Joash of Judah.

verses.note: named as one of the two servants who killed Joash of Judah

characters.name: Jehoahaz, king of Israel

verses.note: reigns seventeen years; the LORD delivers Israel into the hand of Hazael and Benhadad because of the sins of Jeroboam
besought the LORD, who gave Israel a deliverer (unnamed in the text) so that they escaped Syria's hand

funFacts: NAMING COLLISION FLAG: a wholly different 'Jehoahaz' — king of Judah, son of Josiah — appears far later in this same book (2 Kings 23:31). Different kingdom, different man, roughly eighty years apart, same name.

characters.name: Jehoash (Joash), king of Israel

verses.note: weeps over the dying Elisha, shoots an arrow of the LORD's deliverance eastward, then strikes the ground with arrows only three times, limiting his future victories over Syria to three
recovers the cities his father lost to Benhadad, defeating him three times as Elisha foretold
defeats Amaziah of Judah in battle at Beth-shemesh after Amaziah's provocation, breaks down part of Jerusalem's wall, and takes hostages and temple treasure

funFacts: Corrected per adversarial review: earlier drafting had mistakenly attached him as a submanager under Elisha as well as giving him his own tier — a schema contradiction. He is a full manager only; his arrow-ritual scene with Elisha is documented here, on his own tier, not duplicated as a submanager entry.

verses.note: executes his father's assassins but spares their children, citing the law of Moses
defeats Edom in the Valley of Salt and captures Selah (Sela), renaming it Joktheel
provokes Jehoash of Israel to battle and is defeated and humiliated
killed in a conspiracy at Lachish, brought back to Jerusalem for burial

characters.name: Jeroboam (II), king of Israel

verses.note: reigns forty-one years and restores the border of Israel, according to the word of the LORD spoken by Jonah the son of Amittai
recovered Damascus and Hamath for Israel

funFacts: Text never numbers him 'II' — that is a scholarly convention to distinguish him from the earlier Jeroboam of 1 Kings; not asserted here as scripture's own wording.

characters.name: Jonah, the son of Amittai

genealogy.note: Same name and patronymic as the prophet of the book of Jonah — the patronymic match is an explicit textual link, not a mere traditional association.

verses.note: his earlier word that Israel's border would be restored is fulfilled through Jeroboam II

funFacts: 2 Kings itself only cites his prophecy of restoration; it does not narrate any of the events of the book of Jonah.

characters.name: Zachariah, king of Israel

verses.note: reigns six months; killed by Shallum 'before the people', ending the dynasty of Jehu in fulfillment of 2 Kings 10:30

funFacts: KJV spells this name 'Zachariah' (not 'Zechariah') at both its occurrences within 2 Kings (here and at 18:2) — flagged as a different spelling and a different man from 'Zechariah' the writing prophet or other Zechariahs elsewhere in scripture.

characters.name: Shallum, son of Jabesh

verses.note: conspires against and kills Zachariah, then reigns
reigns a full month in Samaria before being killed by Menahem

funFacts: NAMING COLLISION FLAG: a different 'Shallum' — husband of Huldah the prophetess, keeper of the wardrobe — appears later in this same book (2 Kings 22:14). Different man, same book.

verses.note: kills Shallum and reigns; smites Tiphsah and its coasts with great cruelty for not opening to him
pays a thousand talents of silver to Pul, king of Assyria, exacting it from the wealthy men of Israel, 'that his hand might be with him to confirm the kingdom'

genealogy.note: 2 Kings 15:19 names him simply 'Pul, king of Assyria.' A separate figure, 'Tiglathpileser', is named a few verses later (15:29) and again in ch. 16. 1 Chronicles 5:26, a different book, identifies Pul and Tiglath-pileser as the same king — 2 Kings itself never states this identification, so it is treated here as a cross-book identification, not a same-book fact.

verses.note: receives a thousand talents of silver tribute from Menahem of Israel

characters.name: Tiglathpileser, king of Assyria

genealogy.note: See the note on Pul above regarding the cross-book (1 Chronicles 5:26) identification of these two names, which is not asserted here as 2 Kings' own claim.

verses.note: takes Ijon, Abelbethmaachah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead, Galilee, and all the land of Naphtali from Pekah of Israel, carrying the people captive to Assyria
answers Ahaz of Judah's appeal for help against Syria and Israel, takes Damascus, and kills Rezin

funFacts: KJV renders his name as one word, 'Tiglathpileser'.

verses.note: reigns two years; killed in the palace at Samaria by his own captain Pekah, aided by Argob and Arieh and fifty Gileadites
a captain of Pekahiah who conspires against and kills him, then reigns
loses much of Israel's territory to Tiglathpileser
killed by Hoshea son of Elah in a conspiracy
allies with Rezin of Syria to besiege Ahaz in Jerusalem
joins Pekah of Israel in besieging Ahaz at Jerusalem, but they are not able to overcome it
recovers Elath to Syria
killed by the king of Assyria (Tiglathpileser) after Ahaz's appeal for help

characters.name: Hoshea, son of Elah

genealogy.note: His father, also named Elah, is a different person from King Elah of Israel in 1 Kings 16 (a different book, an earlier king) — flagged to avoid confusion between the name Elah used as a patronymic here and as a royal name there.

verses.note: conspires against, kills, and succeeds Pekah
becomes a servant/tributary to Shalmaneser, then conspires with 'So king of Egypt' and withholds tribute
the king of Assyria shuts him up and binds him in prison

funFacts: The last king of the northern kingdom of Israel; his rebellion is the direct trigger for the siege that ends the kingdom, though the siege itself is Shalmaneser's own act (17:5-6).

characters.name: Shalmaneser, king of Assyria

genealogy.note: 2 Kings gives no patronymic for this king; identified only as 'Shalmaneser king of Assyria'.

verses.note: comes up against Hoshea, who becomes his servant and pays tribute
discovers Hoshea's conspiracy with Egypt and imprisons him
besieges Samaria for three years and personally takes it, carrying Israel away captive to Assyria — the event that ends the kingdom of Israel
the fall of Samaria is retold in summary within Hezekiah's regnal account

funFacts: Given a full manager tier per adversarial review — the foreign king whose own action personally ends the northern kingdom, comparable in narrative weight to Sennacherib and Nebuchadnezzar, both of whom already carry full tiers.

verses.note: 'made his son to pass through the fire, according to the abominations of the heathen' — the son is not named
appeals to Tiglathpileser of Assyria for help against Syria and Israel, sending temple and palace silver and gold as a present
sees an altar at Damascus, sends its pattern to Urijah the priest, and has a copy built in the temple, displacing the bronze altar

characters.name: Hezekiah, king of Judah

genealogy.note: 'Zachariah' here is a different man from Zachariah son of Jeroboam II (15:8) and from Zechariah the writing prophet — a recurring name in this book worth flagging each time.

verses.note: removes the high places, breaks the brasen serpent Moses had made, which Israel had been burning incense to
Sennacherib invades and Hezekiah strips the temple and his own treasury to pay tribute
spreads Sennacherib's threatening letter before the LORD in the temple and prays
falls sick, is granted fifteen more years of life, and given the sign of the sundial of Ahaz going backward ten degrees
shows all his treasures to envoys of Berodachbaladan, son of Baladan, king of Babylon

funFacts: Uses the KJV's own spelling 'Berodachbaladan' (20:12) — distinct from the parallel account's spelling in Isaiah 39:1, a different book.

genealogy.note: 2 Kings does not give his father; 19:37 names his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer as his assassins, and Esarhaddon as his successor.

verses.note: invades Judah and takes its fenced cities
sends Tartan, Rabsaris, and Rabshakeh with a great army against Jerusalem
the angel of the LORD smites 185,000 in the Assyrian camp in one night
returns to Nineveh and is later killed by his own sons while worshipping in the house of Nisroch his god

characters.name: Rabshakeh
characters.perkNote: Sennacherib's own spokesman, delivering his threats directly and at length.

genealogy.note: 'Rabshakeh' (like 'Tartan' and 'Rabsaris' alongside him) is an Assyrian court title/office, not a personal name — KJV capitalizes it like a proper noun, but it denotes a rank.

verses.note: delivers a lengthy taunting speech to Hezekiah's officials and the people on the wall, in Hebrew, mocking trust in the LORD and in Egypt
returns to Sennacherib, finding him warring against Libnah
tells Hezekiah's servants not to be afraid of Sennacherib's words and prophesies his downfall
delivers a long oracle against Sennacherib and a promise of deliverance for Jerusalem
tells the sick Hezekiah to set his house in order, for he shall die
prescribes a lump of figs laid on Hezekiah's boil, and he recovers
prophesies that Hezekiah's treasures and descendants will be carried to Babylon

characters.name: Manasseh, king of Judah

verses.note: rebuilds the high places Hezekiah destroyed, builds altars to Baal, worships the host of heaven, and sets a carved image in the temple itself
makes his son pass through the fire, uses divination and enchantments, deals with familiar spirits and wizards
sheds very much innocent blood in Jerusalem
the text itself names Manasseh's sins as the specific reason the LORD would not pardon Judah, directly connecting his reign to the eventual exile

funFacts: Given a full manager tier despite a relatively short account, because the text itself repeatedly and explicitly cites his reign as the theological hinge explaining Judah's later fall (21:10-15; 23:26-27; 24:3-4) — a genuinely load-bearing figure, not merely a name in a list.

genealogy.mother: Meshullemeth, the daughter of Haruz of Jotbah

verses.note: reigns two years, following his father's evil ways
his own servants conspire and kill him; 'the people of the land' then kill the conspirators and make Josiah king in his place

characters.name: Josiah, king of Judah

genealogy.mother: Jedidah, the daughter of Adaiah of Bozkath

verses.note: orders temple repairs, appointing Shaphan the scribe to oversee the silver
Hilkiah the priest finds the book of the law; Shaphan reads it to the king, who tears his clothes in distress
sends to inquire of Huldah the prophetess, who confirms coming judgment but promises Josiah himself will die in peace, not seeing the evil
reads the book of the covenant to all the people and leads a covenant renewal
purges idolatrous priests, high places, and vessels across Judah and even into former Israelite territory (Bethel)
killed in battle at Megiddo by Pharaohnechoh of Egypt

funFacts: The book of the law's reforms are enacted personally by Josiah himself — he tears his own clothes, personally leads the covenant renewal and the purge — so this is treated as his own manager tier's narrative content rather than a separate law-type tier.

characters.name: Hilkiah, the high priest
characters.perkNote: Finds the book of the law that sets Josiah's reform in motion.

verses.note: 'I have found the book of the law in the house of the LORD', delivered to Shaphan
commanded by Josiah to remove idolatrous vessels from the temple

characters.name: Shaphan, the scribe
characters.perkNote: Reads the newly found book of the law aloud to Josiah, prompting his response.

verses.note: receives the book from Hilkiah and reads it before the king

characters.name: Huldah, the prophetess
characters.perkNote: Confirms the book's authority and Josiah's own sincerity, informing the direction of his reform.

genealogy.note: Wife of Shallum, keeper of the wardrobe — a different Shallum from the earlier king of Israel by that name (2 Kings 15:10-15).

verses.note: dwelt in Jerusalem in the college; the king's men come to inquire of her
prophesies coming judgment on Judah for its idolatry, but that Josiah himself will be gathered to his grave in peace

funFacts: NAMING COLLISION FLAG: her husband Shallum shares his name with the earlier king of Israel, Shallum son of Jabesh (15:10-15) — different men, same book.

characters.name: Pharaohnechoh, king of Egypt

verses.note: goes up against the king of Assyria at the river Euphrates; kills Josiah at Megiddo when Josiah goes against him
deposes Jehoahaz, puts Judah under tribute, and makes Eliakim king in his stead, renaming him Jehoiakim

funFacts: KJV spells his name as one compound word, 'Pharaohnechoh'.

characters.name: Jehoahaz, king of Judah

genealogy.mother: Hamutal, the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah
genealogy.note: This 'Jeremiah of Libnah' is a different man from the prophet Jeremiah — a common name, no textual link between them.

verses.note: begins to reign; reigns three months in Jerusalem
put in bands by Pharaohnechoh at Riblah, then carried to Egypt, where he dies

funFacts: NAMING COLLISION FLAG: a different, unrelated 'Jehoahaz' — king of Israel, son of Jehu — appears much earlier in this same book (2 Kings 13:1-9).

genealogy.mother: Zebudah, the daughter of Pedaiah of Rumah
genealogy.note: Originally named Eliakim; renamed Jehoiakim by Pharaohnechoh (23:34).

verses.note: taxes the land to pay the silver and gold demanded by Pharaohnechoh
becomes Nebuchadnezzar's servant for three years, then turns and rebels against him
the LORD sends bands of Chaldees, Syrians, Moabites, and Ammonites against him

characters.name: Jehoiachin, king of Judah

genealogy.mother: Nehushta, the daughter of Elnathan of Jerusalem

verses.note: begins to reign; reigns three months in Jerusalem
surrenders to Nebuchadnezzar in the king of Babylon's eighth year
the temple treasures are cut in pieces and taken; Jehoiachin, his mother, wives, officers, and the craftsmen and smiths of Jerusalem are carried captive to Babylon
in the thirty-seventh year of his captivity, Evilmerodach lifts up his head, brings him out of prison, and gives him a daily allowance for the rest of his life

funFacts: His surrender opens the major deportation of Judah's elite; his release under Evilmerodach forms the book's final scene, bookending the exile.

characters.name: Zedekiah, king of Judah

genealogy.mother: Hamutal, the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah
genealogy.note: Full brother of Jehoahaz (same father and mother); uncle of Jehoiachin, whom he succeeded — 'made Mattaniah his father's brother king in his stead' (24:17). Originally named Mattaniah; renamed Zedekiah by Nebuchadnezzar.
children: unnamed sons, slain before him at Riblah (2 Kings 25:7)

verses.note: made king by Nebuchadnezzar in Jehoiachin's stead, and renamed from Mattaniah
rebels against the king of Babylon

Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem beginning in Zedekiah's ninth year, tenth month; the famine prevails by the ninth day of the fourth month of his eleventh year — a siege of roughly eighteen months by the text's own regnal-year dating, not 'over two years'
the city wall is breached; Zedekiah flees but is overtaken near Jericho; his sons are slain before his eyes, then his own eyes are put out, and he is carried to Babylon in chains

funFacts: Corrected per adversarial review: the siege duration is stated here as roughly eighteen months, matching the text's own ninth-year/tenth-month to eleventh-year/fourth-month dating, not the earlier draft's 'over two years'.

genealogy.note: 2 Kings does not state his father. His relationship to Evilmerodach, his successor named at 25:27, is likewise not stated within 2 Kings itself — see Evilmerodach's own entry for the hedge on that point.

verses.note: comes up against Jehoiakim, who becomes his servant for three years
besieges Jerusalem; Jehoiachin surrenders to him
makes Mattaniah (Zedekiah) king in Jehoiachin's stead
in his nineteenth year, his servant Nebuzaradan burns the house of the LORD, the king's house, and every great house in Jerusalem

characters.name: Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard
characters.perkNote: Personally carries out Nebuchadnezzar's destruction and deportation orders in Jerusalem.

verses.note: burns the temple, the king's house, and all the great houses of Jerusalem, and breaks down the city walls
carries away the rest of the people, but leaves some of the poor of the land as vinedressers and husbandmen
seizes the chief priest, the second priest, and other officials, who are put to death at Riblah

genealogy.note: Grandson of Shaphan, per 'Gedaliah the son of Ahikam' (25:22); Ahikam is likely the same Ahikam who protected Jeremiah in the parallel Jeremiah account, but that identification is not made within 2 Kings itself and is not asserted here.

verses.note: appointed governor over the remnant left in the land by Nebuchadnezzar
tells the remaining captains and people not to fear the Chaldees, to serve the king of Babylon, and it shall be well with them
killed by Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, of the royal seed, along with the Jews and Chaldees who were with him at Mizpah

characters.name: Ishmael, son of Nethaniah

genealogy.note: Described as 'of the seed royal' (25:25), i.e. of the Davidic line.

verses.note: comes with ten men and kills Gedaliah, along with the Jews and Chaldees at Mizpah

funFacts: After this, 'all the people, both small and great... arose, and came to Egypt: for they were afraid of the Chaldees' (25:26), closing the narrative before the book's final scene of Jehoiachin's release.

characters.name: Evilmerodach, king of Babylon

genealogy.note: 2 Kings 25:27 never states that Nebuchadnezzar is his father — that parentage is extra-biblical historical knowledge (commonly assumed since he is Nebuchadnezzar's known historical successor), not a claim this book itself makes. Left explicitly hedged rather than asserted as flat fact.

verses.note: in the year he began to reign, lifts up the head of Jehoiachin out of prison, speaks kindly to him, sets his throne above the thrones of other captive kings in Babylon, and gives him a continual daily allowance for the rest of his life

funFacts: KJV spells his name as one compound word, 'Evilmerodach'.
The book's final scene — closing on an act of mercy toward the exiled line of David, rather than on judgment.

characters.name: Hazael

genealogy.note: Sent as a servant/messenger of Ben-hadad king of Syria (2 Kings 8:7-9) before becoming king himself; no prior royal lineage is given for him in the text — Elisha weeps because he foresees Hazael, a commoner by the text's own framing, becoming king and doing great harm to Israel (8:12-13).

verses.note: Sent to ask Elisha if Ben-hadad will recover from sickness; Elisha weeps, foreseeing the evil Hazael will do to Israel; Hazael returns and smothers Ben-hadad with a wet cloth, then reigns in his place.
Wounds Jehoram of Israel in battle at Ramothgilead.
'In those days the LORD began to cut Israel short' — Hazael conquers all the land east of Jordan, from Gilead to Bashan.
Takes Gath and sets his face toward Jerusalem; Joash of Judah pays him off with the temple and palace treasures to turn him back.
'The LORD delivered them into the hand of Hazael king of Syria... all the days of Jehoahaz' — oppresses Israel through that whole reign.
Dies; succeeded by his son Ben-hadad. Jehoash of Israel recovers the cities Hazael had taken from Jehoahaz, per Elisha's dying arrow prophecy.

funFacts: Naming collision flag: his son and successor is also called 'Ben-hadad' (13:24) — a THIRD man by that name across this book and 1 Kings, distinct from both the earlier Ben-hadad of Asa's reign and the Ben-hadad besieging Samaria under Ahab/Jehoram.
Elisha's weeping over what Hazael will do (8:11-13) is one of the few places in either Kings book where a prophet reacts with open grief to a foreseen future rather than just announcing it.

genealogyLists.seventy_sons_of_ahab: 2 Kings 10:1-7 — seventy sons of Ahab in Samaria, killed by the elders/rulers of the city at Jehu's instruction; none individually named.
genealogyLists.forty_two_brethren_of_ahaziah: 2 Kings 10:12-14 — forty-two 'brethren of Ahaziah' (kinsmen of the royal house of Judah) met and slain by Jehu at the pit of the shearing house; none individually named.
genealogyLists.captains_of_hundreds_jehoiada_coup: 2 Kings 11:4-10, 15 — the captains over hundreds, of the Carites and of the guard, who carry out Jehoiada's coup against Athaliah; none individually named.
genealogyLists.sons_of_the_prophets: Recurring unnamed groups across Elisha's ministry (e.g. 2 Kings 2:3-7, 15-18; 4:1, 38-41; 6:1-7) — company/companies of prophets associated with Elisha at Bethel, Jericho, and Gilgal.
genealogyLists.foreign_peoples_resettled_in_samaria: 2 Kings 17:24 — people from Babylon, Cuthah, Ava, Hamath, and Sepharvaim, settled in Samaria by the king of Assyria after the fall of Israel; described corporately, not individually.
genealogyLists.people_of_the_land: Recurring corporate actor across the book (e.g. 2 Kings 11:14, 11:18-20; 21:24; 23:30) — 'the people of the land', acting collectively at several points including Amon's death and Josiah's and Jehoahaz's accessions; never an individually named figure.
genealogyLists.officials_and_craftsmen_deported_with_je: 2 Kings 24:14-16 — princes, mighty men of valour, craftsmen, and smiths (ten thousand plus a thousand more per the text's own two tallies) carried captive to Babylon with Jehoiachin; none individually named.
genealogyLists.poor_left_as_vinedressers: 2 Kings 25:12 — 'certain of the poor of the land' left behind by Nebuzaradan as vinedressers and husbandmen after the fall of Jerusalem; not individually named.
genealogyLists.hazael_note: hazael (referenced as scribeTiers tier 11 managerId) genealogy note: 2 Kings gives no patronymic for Hazael — 8:15 states only that he reigned in Benhadad's stead after smothering him; treated as a manager tier for his sustained cross-reign significance (2 Kings 8, 10, 12, 13) even though his own personal genealogy is unstated.
